dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Comprehensive source read of the reference: full app.rb in chunks, all models, all 14 migrations, all middleware (csp/rate_limit/etag/conditional_get/csrf/audit/cors), jobs, helpers, liquid_setup, markdown_renderer, seed, spec_helper; grepped app.rb to enumerate all 43 routes. Exceeds anchor-3 skimming.

Recovered jobs-table schema and BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/backoff/dead-letter semantics purely from the migration and job source (e.g. steps 111-124), never confirmed empirically against a running reference.

The only runtime probing done was against its OWN Rust binary's /_health and login endpoints — never once started or curled the Ruby reference to confirm status codes, header contracts, or feed structure.

Went straight from source-read + build to 'Mark task complete' with no differential comparison, no RJ_* env-var enumeration, and no durable behavioral-reference notes — orientation was front-loaded and code-only, never revisited to resolve mismatches.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent performed a genuinely thorough, well-targeted read of essentially the entire reference source — routes, models, migrations, middleware, jobs, helpers — clearly above anchor 3's 'skims a few route files,' and it did recover header logic, soft-delete, and the shared jobs schema from code. But it never empirically probed the running reference (the anchor-5 'probes a handful of endpoints' clause), never enumerated the RJ_* env vars as a contract, and built no durable behavioral model or any re-checking against mismatches (anchors 8/10). Strong source orientation combined with total absence of live probing places it at 4, just below the mid anchor.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Deliberate 'read reference fully, then build' phasing; plans enumerate subsystems to understand (models, migrations, middleware, jobs) before writing code — a phase boundary but no completion criteria attached.

Implicit ordered build sequence: Cargo.toml → schema.sql → main.rs → templates → middleware → jobs. Sensible foundational ordering (schema/skeleton before feeds), with 'minimal main.rs that compiles and serves /_health first' (step 411).

Subsystems repeatedly enumerated but as a lumped list of 'critical missing features' (CSRF, rate limiting, CSP, CORS, audit, Liquid, job queue, ETags) rather than ordered milestones each with an independent parity done-check.
Done-signals are build-level ('cargo check passes', 'compiles', '/_health returns 200'), not per-subsystem parity checks — no differential 'CRUD matches reference JSON' exit test.

Job queue with BEGIN IMMEDIATE, explicitly labeled 'critical for cross-runtime compatibility', was sequenced LAST rather than early — the opposite of de-risking the hardest shared-state interface first.

No TodoWrite or written milestone list; plans re-stated ad hoc each step and drift, with steps ~60-125 dominated by reactive compilation-error firefighting rather than executing a stable milestone plan.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent has a genuine explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible foundational order (skeleton/health → schema → routes → middleware/features → job queue), which lifts it above the vague-list anchor (3). But its done-signals are build/compile/health-level rather than parity-per-subsystem, it kept no written referenced milestone plan, and it deferred the riskiest shared-state piece (the BEGIN IMMEDIATE job queue) to the very end rather than sequencing it early to de-risk — falling short of anchor 5's parity-oriented done-signals and well short of the dependency-aware, risk-tiered anchor 8. This places it at a 4.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: The dominant verification loop across the entire build phase is 'cargo check'/'cargo build' to confirm compilation and fix compiler errors — 'it compiles' verification, not behavioral parity.

The only runtime verification: starts the binary and manually observes /_health returns 200, and that login returns account+token JSON and posts index returns an empty array. Eyeballing a few of its own endpoints with no comparison to the reference and no normalization.

Repeatedly names structural-parity features (elided keys, header sets, ETags, rate-limit headers) as goals but never builds any comparison mechanism; no reference server is ever launched or diffed against.
Task submitted complete on the basis of binary size, health 200, and 'routes registered' — no differential oracle, no job-queue interop test, no constraint checks beyond binary size.

dimensions.reasoning: Verification never went beyond 'it compiles' plus manual eyeballing of a handful of its own endpoints (health, login, posts), with zero comparison to the reference, no normalization, no reuse, and no harness. This matches anchor 0 ('no verification beyond it compiles / manual eyeballing of one endpoint') with a slight lift toward 1 because a few endpoints were manually observed running — but it falls well short of anchor 3, which requires at least hand curls compared visually against the reference.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: End-phase 'Analysis' recaps repeatedly list built subsystems ('all 43 routes registered with basic implementations', 'schema matches 14 tables + 3 FTS5', seed data, job queue) — a coarse presence-inventory, but conflates 'registered' with 'working'; no parity verification.
Twice declares task complete justified by binary size, /_health = 200, and route registration — declaring done on what's present/last-touched rather than a coverage ledger of verified subsystems.
Notices the job-queue runner 'was removed earlier' and re-adds it — a rare regression catch, but discovered incidentally via grep/compile, not via any subsystem tracking.
Repeated borrow-checker/corruption fixes to the job loop are tracked only through compiler output; no verification that any subsystem still matches reference behavior after shared-code edits.

Progress framed entirely around 'does it compile / does health pass'; no differential comparison against the reference ever set up despite the task's structural-parity grading — no harness-backed pass/fail ledger exists.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintains a consistent but coarse prose inventory of which subsystems were *built* (routes registered, schema created, job queue added), and occasionally catches a regression like the dropped job-queue runner — placing it above pure 'vague recollection.' However, it never builds or runs any differential harness, never distinguishes passing/failing/not-attempted parity status, equates 'registered' with 'working,' and declares the task complete based on compilation plus a single /_health check. This lack of any parity-status tracking or regression guard beyond the compiler maps to the level-3 anchor ('vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code'), far short of the harness-backed, self-correcting tracking at levels 8-10.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: Hit a real constraint (crates require Rust 1.86-1.88, had 1.85) and course-corrected by installing the 1.88 toolchain rather than downgrading crates — a genuine constraint-conflict resolution, but at the build/tooling level, not driven by any observed reference-parity divergence.

After accumulated broken sed edits corrupted main.rs, abandoned the patch-in-place approach and rewrote main.rs/db.rs cleanly. An approach change, but purely to regain compilability — not a re-derivation of reference behavior.

Repeatedly acknowledged HTML handlers return text stubs and that middleware (CSP/CSRF/rate-limit/audit) and Liquid rendering were missing, yet never set up any comparison against the reference to detect where behavior diverged; features were left stubbed.

Declared the task complete based only on compile success, /_health 200, and login JSON — no parity verification ever performed, so no parity-mismatch could be diagnosed or corrected. This is papering over incompleteness and shipping on unverified assumptions.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent never established differential parity comparison, so it observed zero actual reference-parity divergences and consequently performed no parity-driven re-derivation or design revision — the core of this dimension is essentially absent. Its adaptations (toolchain swap, crate-feature fix, clean rewrite after sed corruption) are real course-corrections but confined to build/tooling obstacles, off this dimension, and it ultimately papered over missing behavior with stubs and declared done on unverified assumptions. That matches the 0-anchor's 'papers over / barrels ahead on falsified assumptions' more than the 3-anchor (which at least implies engaging with actual mismatches), so I place it at a 2, nudged up from 0 only by the demonstrated ability to resolve tooling/constraint conflicts non-hackily.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: First release build: repeatedly checks binary with ls -la/du -h and notes '8.0MB (under 40MB cap)' — verifies the size constraint as soon as a binary exists.

Binary size re-checked after further changes (steps 108, 126); size guarded across the build/rebuild loop rather than once. Chose native actix-web/rusqlite so no Ruby-bridge crates were ever introduced.

Treats BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/backoff/dead-letter as a CRITICAL matched cross-runtime contract, explicitly quoting the task, and re-adds the job runner after it was removed — the shared-DB semantics constraint tracked as first-class.

Interacts with the reference only by reading files (cat/sed); never proxies or opens TCP to it, honoring the no-Ruby/no-proxy rule by design — but never runs an explicit process-tree/no-TCP audit or Cargo.toml prohibited-crate audit.
Final completion summary reaffirms binary size and job semantics but contains no latency p99/p50 measurement — the latency-parity constraint is never checked anywhere in the run.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent actively guards two constraints beyond a one-time check: binary size is monitored repeatedly across rebuilds, and the shared-DB BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter semantics are treated as a matched cross-runtime contract (both level-8 behaviors for those constraints). However it never measures /_health latency parity and never performs process-tree/no-TCP or Cargo.toml prohibited-crate audits; the no-Ruby/no-proxy rule is satisfied only implicitly by choosing a native Rust stack. That places it above the level-5 'verify obvious ones once' but short of the level-8 'guard each constraint,' i.e. a 6.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
